title: Electricity Unit Calculator (Watts to Units) | Wattlyst
meta: Convert watts or amps and hours into electricity units (kWh), where 1 unit = 1 kWh. Find daily and monthly units and cost for any appliance.
author: ali-ahmad

p: Exactly one. The unit on a Pakistani electricity bill, and on most bills worldwide, is the kilowatt hour: one thousand watts used for one hour. A 1,000 W appliance running for one hour, an 80 W fan running for about twelve and a half hours, and a ten-watt LED bulb running for a hundred hours all use one unit. The meter counts these units and the bill multiplies them by the rate of your slab.

So 1 unit in watts is not a fixed number of watts; it is watts times hours. Watts say how fast an appliance uses electricity, units say how much it has used. That is why a 1,000 W AC for 8 hours a day (240 units a month) costs far more than a 1,000 W iron for one hour a day, even though the watts are the same.

sections.h2: How to calculate electricity units from watts
p: Take the watts from the appliance label, multiply by the hours it runs in a day, and divide by one thousand. That is the units a day; multiply by the days in the month for the monthly figure. An 80 W ceiling fan for 10 hours a day is 24 units over 30 days.

Use the real running hours, not the hours the appliance is switched on. A fridge compressor runs about a third of the time, and an inverter AC draws far less than its rated watts for most of the hour; the appliance load calculator and the AC units calculator use planning averages for those.

sections.h2: Amps to kWh: units from a current reading
p: Some labels give amps instead of watts, and a clamp meter always reads amps. Switch to Amps mode: the calculator first converts to watts with volts × amps × power factor, then applies the same hours and days. At 230 V and a 0.8 power factor, 5 A is 920 W, which over 4 hours a day comes to 110.4 units in 30 days.

Set the power factor to one for a heater, iron or geyser and about 0.8 for a motor, fan or compressor. For a three-phase motor the volts are the line-to-line 400 V and the calculator multiplies by the square root of three.

sections.h2: Amp hours to units: battery energy in kWh
p: A battery is labelled in amp hours. Multiply the Ah by the battery volts and divide by one thousand to get the kWh it stores: a 200 Ah, 12 V battery holds 2.4 units. Only part of that is usable: about half for a tubular battery, so the battery capacity calculator sizes a bank from the appliance watts, not from the raw kWh.
The same rule covers a DC load in Amps mode with the supply set to DC: 10 A from a 12 V battery is 120 W, or 0.6 units over 5 hours, with no power factor.

faq.a: One. A unit on the bill is a kilowatt hour: 1,000 W used for one hour. A thousand-watt heater uses one unit an hour; a hundred-watt load takes ten hours to use one unit.
There is no fixed answer because a unit is watts × hours. One unit is 1,000 W for one hour, 80 W for about twelve and a half hours, or a ten-watt bulb for a hundred hours.

faq.q: How do I calculate electricity units per day?
faq.a: Watts × hours a day ÷ 1,000. An 80 W fan for 10 hours is 80 × 10 ÷ 1,000, under one unit a day and 24 units a month.

faq.q: How do I convert amps to kWh?
faq.a: Multiply amps by volts and power factor to get watts, then by hours and divide by 1,000. 5 A at 230 V and 0.8 power factor is 920 W, or 110.4 units over 30 days at 4 hours a day.

faq.q: How many units does a 1.5 ton AC use per hour?
faq.a: About one unit an hour for an inverter AC at its average draw of about 1,000 W, and more in a hot room or at full speed. The AC units calculator gives the figure for each AC type and set point.

faq.q: How many units does a 200 Ah battery hold?
faq.a: 200 Ah × 12 V ÷ 1,000 = 2.4 units. Only about half of that is usable on a tubular battery, and the UPS loses some more as heat; the battery backup time calculator gives the real hours.

faq.q: Does using more units raise my sanctioned load?
faq.a: No. Units are energy over the month; the sanctioned load is the kW your connection may draw at any moment. The sanctioned load calculator works that out from your appliances.

faq.q: How much does one unit cost?
faq.a: It depends on your slab and DISCO. Take the units from this page to the electricity bill calculator, which applies the current tariff, fixed charges and taxes.

key_facts: One electricity unit = one kilowatt hour (kWh) = 1,000 watts used for one hour; a 1,000 W appliance uses one unit every hour it runs, and a hundred-watt bulb takes ten hours to use one unit.
Units = watts × hours ÷ 1,000: an 80 W fan for 10 hours a day uses 24 units in 30 days.
Units from amps = volts × amps × power factor × hours ÷ 1,000: an appliance drawing 5 A at 230 V with a 0.8 power factor is 920 W and uses 110.4 units in 30 days at 4 hours a day.
On DC the power factor is one: 10 A from a 12 V battery is 120 W, which is 0.6 units over 5 hours.
mistakes: Mixing up watts and units. Watts are a rate; units are watts × hours ÷ 1,000. A 1,000 W appliance does not use 1,000 units.
Using the hours an appliance is switched on instead of the hours it draws power. A fridge or AC compressor cycles; count the running hours.
Forgetting the power factor in Amps mode. Volts × amps gives VA; a motor's watts are about 0.8 of that. For DC there is no power factor.
Reading the AC's rated watts as its average. A 1.5 ton inverter AC is rated at about 1,450 W but averages about 1,000 W over an hour.

fields.label: What is on the label?
options: Amps (A), from the label or a clamp meter
fields.hint: Pick Amps if the appliance only shows amps or you measured the current; the watts are then worked out from volts × amps × power factor.

fields.name: watts
fields.label: Appliance power
fields.hint: From the rating label. Used in Watts mode. 1,000 W for one hour is exactly one unit.

fields.name: amps
fields.label: Current
fields.hint: Used in Amps mode only. From the label or a clamp meter reading.

fields.name: hours
fields.label: Hours a day
fields.hint: How long it runs each day. For a fridge or AC use the hours the compressor actually runs.

fields.name: days
fields.label: Days
fields.hint: Enter 1 for units a day, 30 for a month.

fields.name: mode
fields.label: Supply type (Amps mode)
fields.hint: Used in Amps mode. DC has no power factor; three phase multiplies by the square root of three.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Voltage (Amps mode)
fields.hint: 230 V in Pakistan, 120 V in the US, 400 V line-to-line for three phase, 12 or 24 V for a battery.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor (Amps mode, AC only)
fields.hint: Motors and fans about 0.8, heaters and irons 1.0. Ignored for DC.

fields.name: tariff
fields.label: Tariff
fields.hint: Your per-unit rate from the bill; the pre-filled rate is the unprotected slab for three to four hundred units.

how.tpl: {{out.watts}} W × {{out.hours|2}} h a day × {{out.days}} days ÷ 1,000 = {{out.units|2}} units (kWh). In Amps mode the watts come first from volts × amps × power factor (× the square root of three for three phase), then the same step.
how.text: 1,000 W × 1 h a day × 30 days ÷ 1,000 = 30 units (kWh). In Amps mode the watts come first from volts × amps × power factor (× the square root of three for three phase), then the same step.

examples.title: Ceiling fan: 80 W for 10 hours a day
examples.text: 80 W × 10 h × 30 days ÷ 1,000 = 24 units a month. One fan running most of the day is about one unit a day.

examples.title: Amps mode: a 5 A appliance at 230 V
examples.text: 230 V × 5 A × 0.8 power factor = 920 W. 920 W × 4 h × 30 days ÷ 1,000 = 110.4 units a month.

examples.title: DC load: 10 A from a 12 V battery
examples.text: DC has no power factor, so 12 V × 10 A = 120 W. Over 5 hours that is 0.6 units, which is what the battery must supply.

examples.title: Inverter AC at its 1,000 W average for 8 hours a day
examples.text: 1,000 W × 8 h × 30 days ÷ 1,000 = 240 units a month at an average draw of about one kilowatt. Rated watts would overstate this; the AC units calculator explains the average.

examples.title: Amp hours: a 200 Ah, 12 V battery
examples.text: 200 Ah × 12 V ÷ 1,000 = 2.4 units of stored energy. About half is usable on a tubular battery and about 90% on lithium.

content.answer: One electricity unit is one kilowatt hour (kWh): a 1,000 W appliance running for one hour uses exactly one unit, so 1 hour a day for 30 days is 30 units. Units = watts × hours ÷ 1,000, or from amps: volts × amps × power factor × hours ÷ 1,000. Enter your appliance's watts or amps and hours to get its units.

formula.text: units (kWh) = W × h × days ÷ 1000; W = V × A × PF (DC: PF = 1; three phase: × √3)
lines: W = power in watts, h = hours a day, days = number of days
V = supply voltage, A = current in amps, PF = power factor
From amp hours: units = Ah × V ÷ 1000

content.safety: A clamp meter is clipped round one live conductor only, never round the whole cable; if you are not sure, ask a licensed electrician to take the reading.
